This is the classic reactive spreadsheet exercise. The stubs in `react.go` define the shape; I'll implement a reactor that tracks cells in creation order (which is a topological order of the dependency graph), so propagation is always correct even with diamonds and shared dependencies.

Note: The reason I used a monotonically increasing callback ID per cell (rather than the slice length) is that if you use the slice length, IDs will collide after deletion, and the wrong callback might end up being deleted. Alright, let's run the tests.

All 13 tests pass. The implementation is entirely in `react.go` (no new files, `react_test.go` untouched):

- **`reactor`** keeps every cell in creation order. Since a compute cell can only depend on cells that already exist, creation order is a topological order of the dependency graph.
- **`cell`** holds a value, an optional `compute` closure (nil for inputs), its direct dependents, and registered callbacks.
- **`SetValue`** returns early if the value didn't change, then collects the transitively affected subgraph via DFS, and recomputes those cells in creation (topological) order — so every dependency is up to date before any dependent reads it. Callbacks fire only when a cell's value actually changes, and exactly once per stable-state transition.
- **`canceler`** removes a callback by a monotonically increasing per-cell ID, which makes `Cancel` idempotent and safe against ID reuse after removals.

This ordering approach is what makes the tricky tests pass: `TestOnlyCallOnceOnMultipleDepChanges` (a cell with multiple changed dependencies fires its callback exactly once) and `TestNoCallOnDepChangesResultingInNoChange` (dependencies change but the output doesn't, so no callback).
